bus.name: Spacecraft bus
bus.short: The body: frame, computer, thrusters, fuel tanks
bus.explain: Every spacecraft has a 'bus': the body that holds everything together. It carries the onboard computer, small thrusters that turn the spacecraft, and the fuel tanks. Always included.

slots.label: Launch vehicle
slots.hint: The rocket that throws your spacecraft into space. Bigger rocket = more mass, more money.

slots.label: Power
slots.hint: Where electricity comes from. Everything on board runs on it.

slots.label: Instruments
slots.hint: The science tools. Pick up to 3. Each one adds mass, power use, cost and data.

slots.label: Comms
slots.hint: The radio that sends your data home. Science that never reaches Earth doesn't count.

parts.name: Light rocket
parts.explain: A two-stage rocket. Rockets drop empty stages on the way up to get lighter: that is how they reach space. A small rocket can only carry a light spacecraft.
parts.similarTo: Class of Delta II, which launched the Spirit and Opportunity rovers

parts.name: Medium rocket
parts.explain: Two stages plus strap-on boosters that burn for the first two minutes and fall away. Enough for most Mars missions.
parts.similarTo: Class of Atlas V, which launched Perseverance and MRO

parts.name: Heavy rocket
parts.explain: Three rocket cores strapped side by side. The side cores separate first. Needed for heavy spacecraft or far targets like Jupiter.
parts.similarTo: Class of Falcon Heavy, which launched Europa Clipper

parts.name: Small solar panels
parts.explain: Panels turn sunlight into electricity. The energy is free, but the farther you go from the Sun, the weaker the light. Dust and darkness stop them.

parts.name: Large solar panels
parts.explain: Bigger wings, more electricity. Still useless in darkness, and weak far from the Sun.

parts.name: RTG (nuclear battery)
parts.explain: A radioisotope generator turns the heat of decaying plutonium into electricity. It works in darkness, dust and far from the Sun for many years. Curiosity, Perseverance and Voyager use one.

parts.name: Camera
parts.explain: Takes sharp pictures: craters, dry riverbeds, cracks in ice. Photos are big files, so a camera makes a lot of data.

parts.name: Spectrometer
parts.short: Tells what rocks are made of
parts.explain: Splits light into colors, like a prism. Every mineral has its own color fingerprint, so it can find minerals that only form in water.

parts.name: Ice radar
parts.explain: Sends radio waves into the ground and listens to the echoes. It can see buried ice and layers kilometers deep. Needs a lot of power.

parts.name: Seismometer
parts.explain: Feels tiny shaking of the ground to learn what is deep inside a world. It must touch the ground, so it only works on a lander.

parts.name: Magnetometer
parts.explain: Measures magnetic fields. A salty ocean under ice changes the magnetic field around a moon. That is how scientists found hints of Europa's ocean.

parts.name: Small antenna
parts.explain: Sends data home by radio. A small antenna spreads its signal wide, so only a little of it reaches Earth: slow downloads.

parts.name: High-gain antenna
parts.explain: A big dish focuses the radio beam into a narrow ray aimed at Earth, like a flashlight instead of a bare bulb. Much faster, but heavier and power-hungry.

parts.name: Heat shield
parts.explain: Falling through air heats a spacecraft to over 1,000 °C. A heat shield protects it while the air slows it down. No air on the Moon or Europa, so no need there.

parts.name: Redundancy kit
parts.explain: A spare computer and spare wiring. If something breaks, the backup takes over. The mission lives 50% longer and survives more accidents.

parts.name: Battery pack
parts.explain: Charges when there is spare power and helps through shadows and storms.
